newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's left tells Clinton: rethink economic ties.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's left tells Clinton: rethink economic ties.

text.p: In contrast to the official government welcome for U.S. President Bill Clinton, Mexico's main leftist opposition party on Wednesday urged Washington to rethink close economic ties with Mexico because of "terrible" results.
The Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), which has gained increased electoral support in recent months, published an open letter to Clinton in several Mexican dailies.
PRD leaders read an English translation of the letter to Clinton in a private meeting with him on Tuesday, the first ever between a U.S. president and Mexican opposition parties.

"It is urgent, we believe, to revise the current economic model of economic integration between Mexico and the United States which produces ... terrible results in both countries: the most serious concentration of wealth in half a century," the PRD letter said.

It also sharply criticised the United States for its history of intervention in Mexico's affairs -- which included grabbing more than half its territory in 1848 -- and said U.S. citizens often held absurd stereotypes about Mexico.

"We keep reiterating the obvious: Mexico is not and cannot be a nation of corrupt officials, drug-traffickers and poor people who migrate illegally to the United States in the hope of reconquering the territory through their unstoppable demographic prowess," it said.

Despite the letter's harsh tone and the clear differences between the stridently leftist PRD and Clinton, PRD leaders on Wednesday described the meeting as warm, and noted it ran about 10 minutes longer than the scheduled 15 minutes.

"It was a very cordial atmosphere, not forced at all...He seemed to me a kind person who has definite opinions and defends them, but is open to dialogue," Ricardo Pascoe, the PRD's head of international affairs, told Reuters.

In the letter, the PRD welcomed the meeting between both sides but said it was long overdue to break with what it termed a tradition of U.S. presidents turning a deaf ear to any voices in Mexico outside the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).
Clinton defended NAFTA during the meeting, but acknowledged with concern the growing gap between rich and poor on both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border, Pascoe said.
During the meeting with Clinton, PRD leaders also vented their concern about abuse against millions of Mexican illegal immigrants in the United States.

"In many cases, certified by human rights groups, excessive force, savagery, is used in roundups of illegals and in their detention," the PRD letter said. Clinton told the leaders he would personally look into the matter, Pascoe said.

Mexico's July midterm elections were not discussed, the official said. Most polls show the PRD candidate Cuauhtemoc Cardenas -- who was in New York during Clinton's visit -- ahead in the first ever race for mayor of Mexico City.
